newsitem.title: GERMANY: German wheat sellers determined to maintain prices.
newsitem.headline: German wheat sellers determined to maintain prices.

text.p: German wheat export sales were seasonally slow but sellers were keeping up prices ahead of business in the new year, brokers said on Wednesday.
"Nominal prices are even a touch higher here or there because sellers need to account for storage costs," one said.
"But I believe there won't be any more sales this year as old business is being carried out and some ships have failed to arrive...this will keep us occupied well into early January."
German prices were also underpinned by higher levels in Britain and France, where markets received a boost from a sale to Egypt, as well as some domestic mill buying.
But early 1997 prices had little upside potential because of feed wheat supply pressure from a number of western European origins, brokers said.
But sellers pointed to possible farmer retention if levels were to fall and latent Polish and Uzbek wheat demand.
Another unknown was the EU's licensing policy after only a third - 477,700 tonnes - of free market wheat export bids were granted last week.
"They could export a lot more and at higher rebates if they wanted...the buyers are certainly there," one broker said.
The Hamburg grain exchange left its bread wheat price (12.5 percent, 220 Hagberg) at 277.50 marks a tonne and raised its spot feed wheat price free Hamburg by 2.50 marks to 272.50.
Export brokers otherwise kept prices broadly unchanged this week.
Normal spot bread wheat (12 percent protein) for first half January was quoted at 284-287.50 marks and higher quality offers were at 290-305, depending on protein levels.
Barley markets took support from some sales to the Netherlands and renewed seller assertiveness after feed grain supply pressure had weighed on post-harvest markets.
Fob barley was quoted at 255-270 marks, up 2.50-7.50 marks.
Fob rye offers were a shade firmer at 252.50-265 marks. --Vera Eckert, Hamburg newsroom, +49-40-41903275
